16-inst.1: Universities recruit athletes with campus tours designed to feel like homecomings.
16-inst.2: When athletes ask about compensation, the institution says "you're getting a free education."
16-inst.3: Universities promise "life after sports" support, then cluster athletes in easy majors.
16-inst.4: The alumni network pulls former athletes back with fundraisers and hall of fame inductions.
16-inst.5: The NCAA invented the term "student-athlete" to avoid classifying athletes as employees.
16-inst.6: The NFL told players the game was safe for decades while discrediting unfavorable researchers.
16-inst.7: College athletes must choose between playing time and the education the scholarship promised.
16-inst.8: Playing time comes on schedules athletes cannot predict, because a secure player has leverage.
16-inst.9: The scholarship required a 2.5 GPA last year and a 2.8 this year, without the athlete's input.
16-inst.10: The NCAA used "amateurism" to keep athletes unpaid while the institutions generated billions.
16-inst.11: Sports organizations that fail to protect athletes blame them: "they signed up for this."
16-inst.12: USA Gymnastics and Penn State silenced and even punished the athletes who reported abuse.
16-inst.13: Students generating billions for a scholarship is defended as tradition, not called extraction.
16-inst.14: The athletic department keeps athletes in separate facilities, schedules, and social circles.
16-inst.15: Conferences and leagues pit schools against each other for rankings, recruits, and revenue.
16-inst.16: Sports media depends on league access, so it amplifies stories that serve the league.
16-inst.17: Athletes who challenge authority get labeled "locker room cancers," toxic to future employers.
16-inst.18: Institutions that covered up abuse say "no comment" until the media cycle moves on.
16-inst.19: Players reach the bargaining "agreement" when they can no longer afford not to agree.
16-inst.20: Team culture turns hazing rituals that are illegal everywhere else into proof of belonging.
16-inst.21: Exhausted players' unions accept that franchise tags and draft systems will never be reformed.
16-inst.22: Teams impose curfews to "ensure recovery" and media limits to "protect the player's focus."
16-inst.23: Institutions call athletes students first, framing their labor as education, not employment.
16-inst.24: The institution makes each athlete a number and a position, with separate housing and dining.
16-inst.25: Sports organizations call the field a cathedral to hide who profits and who suffers.
16-inst.26: Institutions earn billions from athletes and pay them in scholarships worth a fraction of it.
16-inst.27: In a lockout, the league declares an impasse and cancels games to pressure the players.
16-inst.28: Teams trade and waive players like inventory, without counting their wellbeing or families.
16-inst.29: Each recruiting class replaces the last, flowing in like any other industrial supply chain.
16-inst.30: The university calls a forty-thousand-dollar scholarship for four million in labor "education."

16-civ.1: Sports are idealized as the one place where it doesn't matter who you are, only how you play.
16-civ.2: Cities fund stadiums with tax revenue, then watch the owner sell the team for a billion.
16-civ.3: Children with limited options hear "sports is your ticket out," a promise true for one percent.
16-civ.4: Sports media sells comeback stories of aging champions whether or not they serve the body.
16-civ.5: A civilization that worshipped the performance turns a household name into a trivia question.
16-civ.6: The culture calls obedience and tolerance of pain "character" and says sports build it.
16-civ.7: Athletes must sacrifice their bodies or forfeit the only earning window the system offers.
16-civ.8: Sports dynasties rise and fall without pattern, and the unpredictability is the product.
16-civ.9: Each generation of athletes is bigger and faster, and the escalation is sold as evolution.
16-civ.10: Sport promises a "level playing field" while some nations' athletes lack clean water.
16-civ.11: A culture that treats athletes as expendable calls them "entitled" when they ask for pay.
16-civ.12: Athletes who kneel during anthems are told to "shut up and play," as if protest attacked sport.
16-civ.13: A civilization has been trained to cheer the tackle that produces a concussion.
16-civ.14: Athletes are surrounded by millions who know their name and almost no one who knows them.
16-civ.15: Nations feel the loss of a World Cup game as a national wound, in events FIFA controls.
16-civ.16: Fans attack athletes who advocate for better conditions because their identity is the team's.
16-civ.17: Athletes who speak politically have their patriotism challenged as a warning to all the others.
16-civ.18: Society meets retired athletes' brain injuries with momentary concern and permanent inaction.
16-civ.19: The public consents by watching, though it has never been offered sports without exploitation.
16-civ.20: Whole populations bond to their teams so tightly that a player's injury feels like their own.
16-civ.21: Fans, analysts, and athletes themselves repeat that "that's just how sports work."
16-civ.22: Leagues and federations frame their monopoly as the structure that makes competition fair.
16-civ.23: The culture tells athletes to "shut up and play," as bodies rather than thinking humans.
16-civ.24: The culture treats an athlete revealing their full humanity as a surprise rather than the norm.
16-civ.25: Society says "it's just a game" to minimize the brain damage and exploitation of the industry.
16-civ.26: Cities raise taxes to build stadiums owned by billionaires who threaten relocation.
16-civ.27: Doping and gambling scandals become content, because even negative attention is monetizable.
16-civ.28: Retired athletes are discarded with no pension and no support for the brain injuries of sport.
16-civ.29: Each sporting era replaces the last, and the names once chanted are forgotten by the next.
16-civ.30: The industry says "they chose this" about a child identified at seven and funneled through it.

17-inst.1: Universities recruit graduate students to "join the most important research" in the field.
17-inst.2: Universities call the stipend education so they can pay skilled researchers below minimum wage.
17-inst.3: The pipeline produces ten PhDs for every tenure-track job and calls nine "not competitive."
17-inst.4: Endowed chairs and emeritus titles keep retired academics in the institution's orbit.
17-inst.5: Adjuncts teach most college courses for less than minimum wage, with no benefits or offices.
17-inst.6: Facing the replication crisis, the field added statistical requirements, not new incentives.
17-inst.7: "Publish or perish" sacrifices depth for volume, because tenure counts papers, not ideas.
17-inst.8: The reviewer who approved your last paper might reject your next one, so you keep producing.
17-inst.9: Prestige metrics change so often that no researcher knows whether their strategy will work.
17-inst.10: Reviewers reject papers as "not sufficiently novel" by criteria never defined in advance.
17-inst.11: Universities extracting sixty-hour weeks tell students the hours wouldn't matter if they cared.
17-inst.12: Universities criticized for exploiting graduate students say the critics "have an agenda."
17-inst.13: Graduate students defend their own poverty wages: "it's the price of doing what you love."
17-inst.14: A biologist and a philosopher asking the same question may never encounter each other's work.
17-inst.15: Journals pit researchers against each other through impact factor rankings and citation counts.
17-inst.16: Grant panels built by the paradigm evaluate the proposals that challenge it.
17-inst.17: Scientists who speak publicly about the replication crisis are smeared as disgruntled.
17-inst.18: Requests for data on publicly funded research are met with "our processes are proprietary."
17-inst.19: Peer review looks objective, but its reviewers are anonymous and their conflicts undisclosed.
17-inst.20: Departments bond through failed grants and brutal reviews, then reproduce the suffering.
17-inst.21: Whole fields say "peer review is broken but unfixable," each resignation validating the next.
17-inst.22: The review board protects human subjects but also decides which research can be conducted.
17-inst.23: In the academic hierarchy, graduate students defer to everyone and labor flows downward.
17-inst.24: Researchers evaluate each other by h-index before they evaluate each other by idea.
17-inst.25: Universities invoke "the pursuit of truth" to bypass the exploitation in their labor practices.
17-inst.26: A researcher's lab closes if the grant check doesn't arrive, so the funder shapes the research.
17-inst.27: "Funding is being cut" makes a fearful workforce accept conditions it would otherwise resist.
17-inst.28: Each semester, the adjunct who taught three hundred students is replaced by a stranger.
17-inst.29: When a new paradigm arrives, researchers find their expertise turned into historical footnotes.
17-inst.30: A university with a thousand PhDs for a hundred jobs says "we provide education."

17-civ.1: Science is idealized so deeply that questioning its institutions sounds like questioning truth.
17-civ.2: Critics of a finding are told "taxpayers funded this research, how dare you question it."
17-civ.3: "Science will solve it" gives the public permission for present inaction on climate change.
17-civ.4: Scientific conferences renew a community's belief in careers that are financially irrational.
17-civ.5: Legislatures defund the humanities and philosophy as impractical, calling it market efficiency.
17-civ.6: "The science is settled" is used to end a conversation, though science is never settled.
17-civ.7: Citizens who trust science inherit its errors, and those who question it are anti-science.
17-civ.8: Unpredictable breakthroughs renew public faith and justify funding all the unremarkable years.
17-civ.9: The evidence on climate change must be "more certain" whenever it threatens powerful interests.
17-civ.10: "Further research is needed" ends nearly every paper, so not-knowing never justifies action.
17-civ.11: An establishment with a replication crisis calls the public scientifically illiterate.
17-civ.12: Skepticism of industry-funded research is labeled anti-science, making "skeptic" an insult.
17-civ.13: Taxpayers who fund research cannot read the results without paying a journal publisher.
17-civ.14: Jargon and paywalls mean the civilization that pays for science cannot read science.
17-civ.15: Nations racing for AI let "will they get there first?" override the question "should we?"
17-civ.16: Science journalists repeat "trust the science" because their access depends on scientists.
17-civ.17: Consciousness studies are smeared as illegitimate in the name of selectively applied rigor.
17-civ.18: Industries hired scientists to produce doubt about tobacco, and the delay cost lives.
17-civ.19: Scientific consensus can look like independent minds converging when it is shared funding.
17-civ.20: The public bonds to science because the disease terrifies and then the vaccine saves.
17-civ.21: Academics say "you can't change the system" because the system punishes every attempt.
17-civ.22: The establishment controls knowledge in the name of protecting the public from misinformation.
17-civ.23: The scientific institution tells the public "you wouldn't understand the methodology."
17-civ.24: Science positions indigenous knowing and spiritual insight as inferior to its method.
17-civ.25: "Science is self-correcting" leaves every fraud to a self-reformation that never arrives.
17-civ.26: Researchers write and review for free, then their institutions pay publishers to read it.
17-civ.27: "We're falling behind in STEM" funnels more students into programs that overproduce candidates.
17-civ.28: An inconvenient lab is quietly closed, and its scientists learn their field was a budget line.
17-civ.29: Each scientific era replaces the last, but the power structure never changes.
17-civ.30: The establishment says "we followed the scientific method" about conclusions shaped by funding.

18-inst.1: Nonprofits cast themselves as stepping in "where government fails and the market ignores."
18-inst.2: Foundations attach conditions to grants that no nonprofit can refuse without losing funding.
18-inst.3: When 2030 arrives without the outcome, a new plan promises the same outcome by 2035.
18-inst.4: Nonprofits that lost funding win funders back with "we have a new theory of change."
18-inst.5: The person who sets salaries tells nonprofit workers "you don't do this work for the money."
18-inst.6: Nonprofits count dollars raised and people served, not whether the intervention worked.
18-inst.7: Charities are criticized for overhead spending, yet without infrastructure they cannot deliver.
18-inst.8: Unpredictable grant renewals keep nonprofits writing proposals instead of doing the mission.
18-inst.9: Donor expectations shift from collective impact to systems change, and programs pay the cost.
18-inst.10: Grant applications promise to "catalyze systemic change" without ever defining it.
18-inst.11: Nonprofits funded only to manage symptoms blame the political system for the problems.
18-inst.12: Nonprofit whistleblowers are told "you're hurting the people we serve."
18-inst.13: Decades of unsolved problems are normalized with "poverty is complex" and "change takes time."
18-inst.14: Nonprofits that should collaborate instead compete for the same grants, donors, and visibility.
18-inst.15: Funders warn that "this other organization is producing better metrics" to drive competition.
18-inst.16: Charity Navigator rates nonprofits by overhead ratios rather than outcomes.
18-inst.17: Nonprofits that call for wealth redistribution over philanthropy are marginalized as fringe.
18-inst.18: Communities that told evaluators a program wasn't working never hear about their feedback.
18-inst.19: The board approves what the executive recommends, which is whatever funders support.
18-inst.20: For communities served, the caseworker becomes a surrogate parent and the program a lifeline.
18-inst.21: Organizations accept that "our funders won't support systems change."
18-inst.22: Funders call their grant conditions "strategic alignment," turning control into partnership.
18-inst.23: Nonprofits pay staff with master's degrees thirty thousand dollars for "invaluable experience."
18-inst.24: Nonprofits reduce a neighborhood with history and culture to its poverty rate.
18-inst.25: The sector speaks the language of transformation while most of its work only mitigates.
18-inst.26: Donor-advised funds give the wealthy instant tax deductions for money that may sit for years.
18-inst.27: Nonprofits amplify visible disasters for donations while invisible suffering is underfunded.
18-inst.28: The program officer who earned a community's trust is let go when the grant is not renewed.
18-inst.29: Each initiative is replaced before it lasts long enough to produce the change it promised.
18-inst.30: The funder whose conditions blocked root causes says "we funded what was proposed."

18-civ.1: Charity is idealized so deeply that questioning it feels like questioning the impulse to help.
18-civ.2: Wealthy nations attach conditions to aid, so the aid builds compliance instead of independence.
18-civ.3: "Ending poverty in our lifetime" has been promised every decade and has never been fulfilled.
18-civ.4: Every earthquake or famine pulls the population back into the giving cycle.
18-civ.5: Development framing positions entire nations as recipients defined by their needs.
18-civ.6: Development takes credit for decreased poverty that correlates with growth in China and India.
18-civ.7: The public can give to a system that may not work, or not give and abandon the people it helps.
18-civ.8: Development successes are publicized and failures filed away, sustaining the industry.
18-civ.9: The Millennium Development Goals were replaced before anyone evaluated them.
18-civ.10: Every organization in the sector claims to be "making a difference," whether or not it does.
18-civ.11: Nations whose policies created poverty blame "corruption" and "cultural factors" instead.
18-civ.12: Communities that say "we want sovereignty over our own development" are called ungrateful.
18-civ.13: A multi-billion-dollar charity industry beside persistent suffering causes no dissonance.
18-civ.14: Nonprofits clean up the consequences of policy downstream without touching its causes.
18-civ.15: Aid agencies cast themselves as the bridge between the North's generosity and the South's need.
18-civ.16: A celebrity holding a child moves audiences to give without the charity proving it works.
18-civ.17: Critics of charity are asked "so you think we should do nothing?"
18-civ.18: Trillions of dollars over decades have produced little independent evidence of systemic impact.
18-civ.19: The charitable tax deduction steers generosity toward nonprofits instead of political action.
18-civ.20: Media exposes the population to suffering, the giving brings relief, and the cycle repeats.
18-civ.21: "Poverty will always exist" feels to the public not like a belief but like a law.
18-civ.22: Development organizations say "we're empowering" while using their own model and metrics.
18-civ.23: Nations that built civilizations for millennia are told they need Western guidance.
18-civ.24: The label "developing nation" turns colonization and extraction into a stage of progress.
18-civ.25: "Be the change you wish to see" turns the demand for reform into volunteering and donating.
18-civ.26: The Gates Foundation shapes policy and research according to a billionaire's worldview.
18-civ.27: Poverty and hunger generate the urgency that drives the giving, so crises fuel the industry.
18-civ.28: The region at the center of global compassion last year is forgotten once attention moves.
18-civ.29: Structural adjustment gave way to good governance and then market-based solutions.
18-civ.30: After fifty years of unsolved problems, the sector says "we are trying to help."

19-inst.1: Beauty brands tell you "because you're worth it," so you buy worthiness instead of a lipstick.
19-inst.2: Brands sponsor self-esteem campaigns, so criticizing the brand feels like attacking the cause.
19-inst.3: Brands promise "we're redefining beauty" while still needing you to feel not enough.
19-inst.4: Seasonal launches keep the consumer never more than six weeks from the next reason to buy.
19-inst.5: Beauty companies turn "visible pores" into conditions that require their product.
19-inst.6: The beauty industry co-opts the language of body positivity while still selling transformation.
19-inst.7: The industry says women are empowered when they buy, so the power is leased from the brand.
19-inst.8: Last season's celebrated brand is replaced this season, so every brand keeps buying visibility.
19-inst.9: Old ingredients are declared harmful and new ones essential, starting each new product cycle.
19-inst.10: "Clean beauty" and "non-toxic" have no standard definitions a regulator could enforce.
19-inst.11: Companies that profit from body insecurity fund self-love campaigns, posing as the healer.
19-inst.12: Critics who link the beauty industry to eating disorders are told they are "anti-empowerment."
19-inst.13: Botox and fillers are marketed as "lunchtime procedures" you can fit between meetings.
19-inst.14: Shifting beauty standards keep most of the population outside them, and that drives spending.
19-inst.15: Brands split women by age with "this product is for mature skin" to market more precisely.
19-inst.16: Beauty editors and influencers police the standard through content that reads as editorial.
19-inst.17: Critics of the beauty industry are accused of glorifying obesity and opposing self-improvement.
19-inst.18: Requests for ingredient transparency are met with "our formulations are proprietary."
19-inst.19: An influencer post that looks like a genuine recommendation is often a paid placement.
19-inst.20: Fashion makes what felt beautiful last season feel dated, and that cycle is the business model.
19-inst.21: Women repeat "the industry will never change," and each resignation confirms everyone else's.
19-inst.22: Workplace grooming standards call appearance control "maintaining a professional standard."
19-inst.23: Salespeople tell consumers "you might not see it but there's some redness here."
19-inst.24: Beauty standards push people to straighten African hair and surgically alter Asian eyes.
19-inst.25: Brands call your skincare routine "your sacred time" so spending feels like devotion.
19-inst.26: The industry earns hundreds of billions from insecurity, so it cannot let you feel good.
19-inst.27: The beauty industry reframes the biologically inevitable process of growing older as a crisis.
19-inst.28: Last season's essential is this season's embarrassment, and each discard creates a purchase.
19-inst.29: The thin body of the nineties gave way to the curvy body of the tens, each needing new work.
19-inst.30: The beauty industry says "we don't tell people what to do, we offer choices."

19-civ.1: Fashion is idealized as art, so questioning it sounds like opposing self-expression.
19-civ.2: Fashion week is treated as a cultural event, giving the industry immunity from critique.
19-civ.3: The industry promises "beauty from within" and then sells supplements and detoxes.
19-civ.4: Thin brows give way to thick brows, and each reversal invalidates the previous purchase.
19-civ.5: A culture that praises "looking young for your age" makes the older female body disappear.
19-civ.6: Society says "beauty is subjective" while hiring applies the standard with brutal objectivity.
19-civ.7: Rejecting beauty standards brings social penalty, and conforming brings financial extraction.
19-civ.8: The culture rewards beauty unpredictably, keeping everyone in a state of aesthetic vigilance.
19-civ.9: Diverse cultural beauty has been compressed into one global monoculture of desirability.
19-civ.10: The word "beauty" means something different in every culture, so it can sell anything.
19-civ.11: A civilization that built an economy on self-rejection blames individuals for their insecurity.
19-civ.12: Critics of a racist, ageist standard are told the industry is "evolving" and should be thanked.
19-civ.13: Attractive people earn more and receive lighter sentences, and society calls it human nature.
19-civ.14: People spend more time looking at their body in a mirror than feeling it from the inside.
19-civ.15: Western standards exported through media put the colonizing culture's features at the top.
19-civ.16: Mothers pass the standard to their daughters with love: "don't eat that, you'll gain weight."
19-civ.17: Non-Western features are called "exotic" rather than beautiful, mirroring economic power.
19-civ.18: The industry meets rising eating disorders with awareness campaigns instead of accountability.
19-civ.19: A century of advertising installed the beauty standard before anyone could evaluate it.
19-civ.20: The attention that followed the weight loss bonds whole populations to the beauty standard.
19-civ.21: "Beauty standards have always existed" hides that one industry now broadcasts one standard.
19-civ.22: The beauty industry says "we celebrate individuality" while profiting from dissatisfaction.
19-civ.23: The industry treats the natural human face as unfinished, needing its finishing touches.
19-civ.24: The average person knows how they look from the outside better than how they feel inside.
19-civ.25: "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder" shields the industry that exports a global standard.
19-civ.26: The Nigerian woman who bleaches her skin sends money to the nations that exported the standard.
19-civ.27: Cellulite wasn't a concern until it was named, and each new problem area creates a new market.
19-civ.28: The beauty industry discards the elder in the nursing home and every body it cannot sell to.
19-civ.29: The natural look replaced the glamorous look, then the clean look, and rotation is revenue.
19-civ.30: The industry says "we don't create beauty standards, we respond to what people want."

23-inst.1: The end-of-life industry promises "we honor your loved one," making the price feel secondary.
23-inst.2: Funeral homes sell pre-need planning as a gift to your family and keep the investment returns.
23-inst.3: Hospitals promise "we're extending your life" with treatments that extend only function.
23-inst.4: The grief industry re-engages the bereaved with "resources for the anniversary of your loss."
23-inst.5: Nursing homes call residents by their room number rather than their name.
23-inst.6: Hospitals say "we're doing everything we can" while doing everything the billing code allows.
23-inst.7: The dying patient accepts final weeks attached to machines or is judged for giving up.
23-inst.8: Insurance claims are delayed, denied, appealed, and partially paid, adding anxiety to grief.
23-inst.9: End-of-life care keeps adding tests and specialists, measured in billing rather than comfort.
23-inst.10: Advance directives say "heroic measures," which every doctor and family reads differently.
23-inst.11: Hospitals that defaulted to aggressive treatment tell families "you chose to continue."
23-inst.12: The death industry says green burial advocates disrespect tradition and commercialize death.
23-inst.13: Dying in a hospital is the default, and dying at home in your own bed requires a request.
23-inst.14: Most employers give the bereaved five days, so anyone still grieving must grieve in secret.
23-inst.15: Insurers sell policies by promising "your family won't have to worry about the cost."
23-inst.16: Clergy direct the bereaved to specific funeral homes and endorse purchased rituals.
23-inst.17: The funeral industry smears home funerals and green burial as morbid and "not sanitary."
23-inst.18: Questions about funeral markups are met with a compassionate "this is industry standard."
23-inst.19: A grieving family that received the Funeral Rule price list is documented as having chosen it.
23-inst.20: End-of-life nurses stay in a system that underpays them because the work became their identity.
23-inst.21: Doctors who know aggressive treatment isn't serving the patient stay silent to avoid conflict.
23-inst.22: Hospice programs set the medication schedule and the definition of comfort, framed as care.
23-inst.23: The medical system speaks about the dying patient rather than to them.
23-inst.24: The elder who kept a garden now eats food they didn't prepare in a room they didn't choose.
23-inst.25: Hospitals say "we did everything we could" so no one is responsible for the outcome.
23-inst.26: Medicare spends billions in the final weeks of life on treatments that serve the billing.
23-inst.27: "Medicare will be insolvent" is used to justify cutting benefits rather than expanding them.
23-inst.28: The hospital has no mechanism for caring for the family once the patient is gone.
23-inst.29: Hospital death gave way to hospice and palliative care, each with its own billing codes.
23-inst.30: The hospital that kept a ninety-two-year-old on life support says "we followed the directive."

23-civ.1: Death rituals are idealized so that questioning their cost feels like questioning the deceased.
23-civ.2: Corporations entered hospice and enrolled patients who may not be terminally ill for payments.
23-civ.3: "We're working on aging" sustains an industry while people die on the same schedule as ever.
23-civ.4: Memorial Day and the empty holiday chair are when grief marketing is most effective.
23-civ.5: A civilization that worships youth turns its elders into its most expensive liability.
23-civ.6: Grieving families are told "they lived a long life," as if a long life made the loss smaller.
23-civ.7: The civilization chose to deny death, so anyone who wants to prepare has no support.
23-civ.8: Intermittent breakthroughs in longevity keep the population investing in the war against death.
23-civ.9: The acceptable lifespan moved from seventy to eighty to ninety, making earlier deaths failures.
23-civ.10: "Death with dignity" is invoked by both the right-to-die movement and its opponents.
23-civ.11: A civilization that hid death calls advance care planning "the individual's obligation."
23-civ.12: The death positive movement is called morbid by a civilization that profits from avoidance.
23-civ.13: A person who brings up death in conversation is the one who makes the room uncomfortable.
23-civ.14: Death was moved out of the home and hidden behind the doors of the hospital and funeral home.
23-civ.15: The death industry invokes "in this culture, the expectation is" to justify expenditure.
23-civ.16: Movies make the professional funeral the template, so families who deviate feel they failed.
23-civ.17: Society calls the home vigil unsanitary and the family-built casket inadequate.
23-civ.18: Schools and families refuse to discuss death, so the industry remains the default navigator.
23-civ.19: Most people do not know they can wash their own dead and build their own casket.
23-civ.20: The culture installs the fear of death so early that people can't imagine living without it.
23-civ.21: "Everyone dies, what can you do?" is spoken by a population never shown an alternative.
23-civ.22: The death industry says "you need us because death is too complicated" for you to handle alone.
23-civ.23: The culture tells adults "cross that bridge when you come to it," so they arrive with no tools.
23-civ.24: The elder who was once the story-keeper is now a demographic and a cost center.
23-civ.25: "Death is a natural part of life" is a platitude that blocks deeper engagement with mortality.
23-civ.26: The death and aging industries grow on a population afraid to die and unable to afford to live.
23-civ.27: The anti-aging industry declares "aging is a disease" and builds a market on it.
23-civ.28: The dead become a name on a headstone weathering in a field no one walks through.
23-civ.29: The multi-day wake was replaced by the two-hour memorial as death was commercialized.
23-civ.30: The death industry calls its pricing "tradition," though it is younger than the automobile.

24-inst.1: The fossil fuel industry sold extraction as "energy is freedom" and "power for progress."
24-inst.2: A community whose school was funded by the drilling company cannot oppose the drilling.
24-inst.3: The industry promises "net zero by 2050" as a permission slip for continued extraction.
24-inst.4: When a nation moves toward renewables, the industry warns that "energy prices will spike."
24-inst.5: Investors fund a new oil extraction technique faster than a new solar storage system.
24-inst.6: Oil companies knew about climate change by the 1970s and funded denial for half a century.
24-inst.7: Developing nations are lectured on clean energy by nations that industrialized on fossil fuels.
24-inst.8: Environmental regulation is enacted then rolled back, enforced then ignored.
24-inst.9: The emission target meant for 2020 was moved to 2030 and presented as updated ambition.
24-inst.10: Corporate climate pledges "aspire to" and "work toward" goals without committing to them.
24-inst.11: The industry that spent billions preventing regulation blames governments for not acting.
24-inst.12: Indigenous communities asserting treaty rights are called obstacles to economic development.
24-inst.13: Damage that once caused riots now gets "we take our environmental responsibility seriously."
24-inst.14: Lobbyists stand between scientists and politicians, interpreting the data for their clients.
24-inst.15: Fossil fuel companies tell nations "if we can't extract here, we'll extract there."
24-inst.16: Think tanks funded by fossil fuel companies publish industry product as independent analysis.
24-inst.17: Climate scientists have had their emails hacked and selectively quoted.
24-inst.18: Asked what chemicals are in the fracking fluid, companies claim trade secrets.
24-inst.19: The impact assessment is conducted by a firm hired by the company seeking the permit.
24-inst.20: Petrostates are bonded to oil because they were never allowed to develop any other identity.
24-inst.21: Environmental groups say "we have to be pragmatic," helplessness wearing a professional suit.
24-inst.22: Regulatory agencies protect the public while being influenced by the industry they regulate.
24-inst.23: Developing nations are told "they need our guidance to develop responsibly."
24-inst.24: Fishing and farming communities lost their identity when extraction contaminated the water.
24-inst.25: The energy industry calls itself "stewards of the earth" while it extracts and contaminates.
24-inst.26: Fossil fuels receive $7 trillion in subsidy a year, making the alternative cost more.
24-inst.27: "Energy security" is invoked to justify fracking, offshore drilling, and pipelines.
24-inst.28: The forest is logged and left, the mountaintop removed and left, the aquifer drained and left.
24-inst.29: BP invests in solar and Shell in wind, so the transition is managed by those who delayed it.
24-inst.30: ExxonMobil responds to what it knew decades ago by saying "the science was evolving."

24-civ.1: The Industrial Revolution is idealized so questioning it sounds like nostalgia for the cave.
24-civ.2: Cheap fossil energy built modern infrastructure, so leaving it means rebuilding everything.
24-civ.3: "Technology will save us" has been a substitute for changing behavior for fifty years.
24-civ.4: The Paris Agreement was followed by continued growth in fossil fuel investment.
24-civ.5: Indigenous communities that lived sustainably for millennia are devalued as primitive.
24-civ.6: "The science is uncertain" came from the same firms that manufactured doubt about tobacco.
24-civ.7: Society faces climate catastrophe or a transition the industry made as painful as possible.
24-civ.8: A record-breaking fire followed by a wet year keeps the population from sustaining its alarm.
24-civ.9: Two degrees was the limit and 1.5 the aspiration, and now three degrees is being modeled.
24-civ.10: "Clean energy transition" has been repeated for thirty years as fossil fuel use increased.
24-civ.11: Nations with the most historical emissions insist "China and India need to reduce emissions."
24-civ.12: Scientists warning about climate change are called alarmists and enemies of the economy.
24-civ.13: Fires and floods that are not normal at all are called "the new normal."
24-civ.14: Inside climate-controlled buildings, people see the environment as a backdrop they drive past.
24-civ.15: The energy industry says "we need this energy now, we'll figure out clean energy later."
24-civ.16: Petrostate governments block climate agreements in international forums to protect oil revenue.
24-civ.17: Environmentalists are smeared as people who "care more about trees than people."
24-civ.18: The fossil fuel industry knew about climate change and funded its concealment for decades.
24-civ.19: Public transit was defunded until the car was the only choice, then recorded as preference.
24-civ.20: The global economy cannot stop burning fossil fuels without stopping itself.
24-civ.21: A population that believes "it's too late" will not demand the changes the industry fears.
24-civ.22: The industry warns "without us, the lights go off," so the answer is always "not yet."
24-civ.23: People are told only governments and corporations can address climate change, so they wait.
24-civ.24: Our identity as animals has eroded so far that "you are an animal" is received as an insult.
24-civ.25: "God gave us dominion over the earth" is reinterpreted as permission to extract without limit.
24-civ.26: Pension funds invested in oil and gas give society a financial reason to keep burning.
24-civ.27: Carbon markets let corporations keep polluting by purchasing offsets.
24-civ.28: Billionaires who profited from extraction now fund space programs to make Mars the replacement.
24-civ.29: Hunter-gatherers were replaced by farmers, then industrialists, each scaling up the impact.
24-civ.30: The energy industry says "we're just meeting the demand" for a demand it created.

25-inst.1: Car companies sell a dependency product as "the open road" and "go anywhere."
25-inst.2: Auto jobs make the workforce itself oppose any policy that would reduce car dependency.
25-inst.3: "Autonomous vehicles will solve everything" defers public transit investment that works today.
25-inst.4: Recall notices and trade-in offers pull drivers back to the dealership and the upgrade cycle.
25-inst.5: Disinvestment made transit bad, then the badness was used as proof transit doesn't work.
25-inst.6: The auto industry says "we give consumers what they want" after engineering the want.
25-inst.7: Cities that invest in transit face the auto lobby, and cities that don't watch congestion grow.
25-inst.8: The bus that runs every fifteen minutes this year runs every forty-five next, so people drive.
25-inst.9: The bus that ran on time wasn't comfortable, and the comfortable bus didn't have WiFi.
25-inst.10: "Infrastructure investment" sounds like transit but in practice means mostly highways.
25-inst.11: The auto industry that designed the car-dependent city says "if people would just carpool."
25-inst.12: Cities that build bike lanes are accused of "waging war on drivers" by the auto industry.
25-inst.13: Forty thousand traffic deaths a year in the United States are reported as a statistic.
25-inst.14: Cul-de-sacs with nowhere to gather within walking distance are called "a nice neighborhood."
25-inst.15: The auto and oil industries tell workers "the green agenda will destroy auto jobs."
25-inst.16: Developers build subdivisions with no transit access, so every family must buy a car.
25-inst.17: Transit advocates are dismissed with "you can't get Americans out of their cars."
25-inst.18: Requests for accident reports and traffic studies meet delay and institutional resistance.
25-inst.19: Highway hearings scheduled during work hours record public participation as consent.
25-inst.20: Communities defend the highway that brings them business even as it brings pollution.
25-inst.21: City planners know the system is unsustainable, but proposing alternatives ends careers.
25-inst.22: Ride-share apps promise "your ride, your way" while the algorithm controls price and route.
25-inst.23: Jargon excludes residents, and the "expert" analysis always concludes more roads are needed.
25-inst.24: The walkable downtown became a parking lot, and the city built for people now exists for cars.
25-inst.25: "The automobile represents freedom" defends a system of debt, commuting, and congestion.
25-inst.26: Drivers must buy insurance from private corporations, a mandate lobbied for by the insurers.
25-inst.27: "The highway needs expansion" is amplified to serve the highway-construction industry.
25-inst.28: Transportation planning bisects one neighborhood with a highway and cuts another's bus route.
25-inst.29: The streetcar gave way to the bus and the bus to the car, while car dependency stayed.
25-inst.30: The city that ran the highway through the Black neighborhood blames "engineering analysis."
